analysis.investment_thesis: Bata India's EBIT/EV earnings yield is approximately 3.7% (EBIT INR 753 Cr ÷ EV implied by EV/EBITDA of 25.29), less than one-third of the 12% magic formula minimum — it is simply priced for perfection. ROCE of 15.1% also falls short of the 20% threshold, and revenue has compounded at only 4.1% over 9 years.
key_strengths: Exceptional 54.97% gross margin signals real brand pricing power in the affordable-premium footwear segment
Strong and improving FCF: INR 670 Cr in FY25, OCF positive all 5 of 5 years, with minimal capex (INR 73 Cr)
50.16% promoter holding by Bata BV provides strategic stability and retail network expertise
key_risks: Revenue virtually stagnant: FY25 revenue (INR 3,489 Cr) is barely above FY2020 (INR 3,056 Cr) — 6 years of near-zero real growth
Lease liabilities driving finance costs from INR 15 Cr (FY18) to INR 141 Cr (FY25) — Ind AS 116 artificially inflates EBITDA and EV
D2C disruptors and fast-fashion footwear brands eroding Bata's mid-market positioning, especially with urban youth
red_flags: EV/EBITDA of 25.29× and P/E of 50.7× on a business with 4.1% revenue CAGR — extremely overvalued by magic formula standards
Net profit in FY25 (INR 331 Cr) virtually identical to FY2019 (INR 329 Cr) — zero earnings growth over 6 years
Finance costs CAGR of 27.4% over 9 years creates an illusion of operational leverage in EBITDA that does not exist at free cash flow level
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The magic formula demands both cheapness and quality — Bata India is neither cheap enough nor high-ROIC enough. An earnings yield of ~3.7% means you are paying 27x EBIT; Greenblatt's formula considers anything below 6% deeply unattractive. ROCE of 15.1% is decent for a retailer but misses the 20% threshold that distinguishes a truly good business from an average one.

What makes Bata frustrating is that the underlying brand is genuinely strong — 54.97% gross margins prove pricing power — but the combination of stagnant volumes (revenue barely moved in 6 years), a lease-heavy retail model that inflates both costs and asset base, and a premium valuation leaves no room for error. The Magic Formula works by buying good businesses at bad prices; Bata is a mediocre-ROIC business at a very good price for the seller.
